instructions: Independent work. No hints or answer key during testing. Ask for clarification; substantive teaching makes the item assisted and requires a fresh replacement. Three questions per batch. Calculator allowed for arithmetic after writing the exact setup; no solver or answer lookup.

items.objective: Choose and calculate measures of center; explain outlier sensitivity.
items.prompt: For 2, 3, 3, 6, 11, find mean, median, and mode.

items.objective: Choose and calculate measures of center; explain outlier sensitivity.
items.prompt: Replace 11 by 51 in that data. Which changes, the mean or median, and why?

items.objective: Calculate population variance and distinguish it from sample variance.
items.prompt: Treat 0, 3, 6 as a population. Calculate its variance with working.

items.objective: Calculate population variance and distinguish it from sample variance.
items.prompt: Treat those same observations as a sample. Calculate the usual sample variance and explain the denominator.

items.objective: Recover the data’s units and interpret spread without assuming normality.
items.prompt: A population has variance 36 m². What is its standard deviation and unit?

items.objective: Recover the data’s units and interpret spread without assuming normality.
items.prompt: A data set has standard deviation 4. Transform every value by y=3x+7. Find the new standard deviation and explain.

items.objective: Read frequency displays and describe center, spread, skew, and extremes.
items.prompt: Histogram bins [0,10), [10,20), [20,30) have counts 3, 9, 6. Find total count and the fraction below 20.

items.objective: Read frequency displays and describe center, spread, skew, and extremes.
items.prompt: A distribution has a long tail toward low values. Name the skew and explain why the tail matters.

items.objective: Interpret direction and linear strength without inferring causation.
items.prompt: Interpret r=-0.92 in terms of direction and linear strength.

items.objective: Interpret direction and linear strength without inferring causation.
items.prompt: A study finds a positive correlation between shoe size and reading ability in children. Does larger shoe size cause better reading? Give a plausible alternative.

items.objective: Distinguish both, either, and at least one; use changing counts and complements.
